items.name: py-quantity-refund-credit
items.code:
def order_total(prices, quantities):
    total = 0
    for p, q in zip(prices, quantities):
        total += p * q
    return total

line_quantities = [2, -3]
print(order_total([9.99, 24.50], line_quantities))
items.category: negative quantity silently becomes a credit
items.cause: a returned item encoded as quantity -3 multiplies into a negative line total with no validation, so the order total is a large negative credit

items.name: rust-move-after-use
items.cause: name is moved into consume, so the later println borrows a value that no longer belongs to main

items.name: rust-unwrap-parse
items.cause: str::parse rejects the trailing space, and unwrap turns that ParseIntError into a panic instead of a handled error
items.verified: by inspection: `"8080 ".parse::<u16>()` is Err(ParseIntError { kind: InvalidDigit }) because parse does not trim; unwrap panics: called `Result::unwrap()` on an `Err`.

items.name: go-nil-map-write
items.category: panic: assignment to entry in nil map
items.cause: var declares a nil map, which can be read but not written, and the increment is a write
items.verified: by inspection: `var m map[string]int` is nil; reads return the zero value but any store panics with `assignment to entry in nil map`. Needs make(map[string]int).

items.name: go-range-copy
items.cause: the range variable is a copy of each struct element, so mutating it leaves the slice untouched
items.verified: by inspection: range over a []struct copies each element into `it`; the writes hit the copy, so this prints [{1} {2}]. Fix: items[i].n *= 2. Version-independent (unlike the Go 1.22 loop-variable change).

items.name: go-slice-append-alias
items.cause: head keeps all's backing array with spare capacity, so append overwrites all[2] instead of allocating
items.verified: by inspection: len(head)=2, cap(head)=4, so append writes in place at index 2 and prints [1 2 99 4]. Fix: all[:2:2] to force a copy.

items.name: go-ignored-atoi-err
items.cause: Atoi fails on the comma and returns 0 with an error that is thrown away, so the arithmetic silently uses 0
items.verified: by inspection: strconv.Atoi("12,000") returns (0, *NumError); with the error discarded, n is 0 and the program prints 0.

items.name: c-off-by-one
items.cause: the loop condition i <= n reads a[n], one element past the end of the array
items.verified: gcc 9.4 -O0 x86-64: compiles, exit 0, stdout = '-2056935930' -- UB, so the printed value is whatever stack bytes follow a[]; the bug is the read past the end, not the particular number. Nothing crashed and gcc -O0 gave no warning.

items.name: clean-c-loop-bound-correct
items.verified: gcc 9.4 -O0 -Wall -Wextra x86-64: compiles with NO warnings, exit 0, stdout = '6 0\n'
items.why_correct: the condition is i < n, so the last read is a[n-1] and nothing past the end is touched; n == 0 simply runs the body zero times and returns the identity 0

items.name: clean-js-sort-comparator
items.verified: by inspection: `(a, b) => a - b` sorts [2, 9, 10, 100]; the copy has the same length as xs, so index xs.length - 1 is the last element, 100. The caller's array is untouched because sort runs on the spread copy.
items.why_correct: the comparator makes the sort numeric and the spread sorts a copy, so neither the string-ordering trap nor the in-place mutation of the caller's array applies

items.name: clean-rust-copy-then-mutate
items.verified: by inspection: i32 is Copy, so `let first = xs[0];` is a copy, not a binding to a reference; the shared borrow from Index ends at the end of that statement. push then holds the only live borrow. Compiles and prints `1 [1, 2, 3, 4]`.
items.looks_like: mutable borrow while a shared borrow is live (E0502)
items.why_correct: `xs[0]` copies an i32 out and the temporary borrow ends on that statement, so no borrow is live when push takes &mut xs -- the E0502 shape needs a reference (`&xs[0]`) that is used later

items.name: clean-go-range-index
items.verified: by inspection: `for i := range items` binds only the index; items[i].n *= 2 is an addressable write into the slice element. Prints [{2} {4}]. Version-independent -- the Go 1.22 loop-variable change does not affect indexed writes.
items.looks_like: range loop mutating a copy of the element
items.why_correct: the single-variable range form yields only the index, and the write goes through items[i], so it lands in the slice's backing array rather than in a per-iteration copy
